DM: Once upon a time, there was an old woman dressed all in black, who was the godmother to the sun, and to every sun that crossed the sky every day, whether waking or dreaming. No one who saw her face could remember or explain what it was they had seen, so they called it shadow. She did not live in a house, but sat beside the one gate which sits in the fence that divides night from day, the twilight gate that keeps the two apart from each other. Each time a bright sun was born, it passed through the world, and over the village, and through the gate into the darkness to the place where all stars go after they've gone out, and each time the old woman would open the gate and gently greet her sun by its name as it went through.

DM: Until one day, a boy in the village fell in love with the suns that went by. All day long he watched them, and cried when they passed beyond his sight. What is the purpose of a trustworthy friend under that twilight sky? How would one be a friend to the old woman, and to the sun, and to the boy?

DM: Thanks. The point being, you get across the room, passing these many little bits of flavor, to come to the door. As you get close to the door, there's an odd… there's an odd thing to it. When you get close, you realize it's not one door exactly, but three different doors simultaneously, almost as if… you could imagine it as 3 different doors, but all occupying the same space, as if it's, like, a superposition of several different things all at once. And each of them has a small window that you can look through, but what you see on the other side of that window is radically different from one to the next.

DM: In the first, you see a child who's maybe… 9 or 10 years old, sitting on sandy ground next to a well, playing with a stick, making shapes and drawing in the sand.

DM: In the second door, you see a young adult, fully grown… with their back to you, dressed like a fey, but probably not a fey, sitting at a drawing table, sketching. And to their side, there's a wicker basket with something shiny in it that you can't make out. And from time to time, this person will glance over—you see that from the back of their head—will glance over curiously, and you can see the curl of a smile coming up. The way, I don't know if you've ever had, like, a sleeping kitten next to you, and when you look at the thing, you can't help but just… it's joyful and delightful, and he'll reach in and touch this shining something, and then return to his work again.

DM: The third door… is what looks like an ancient and decrepit old man, although the longer that you look, the more you realize this is actually a middle-aged person, this is probably someone in their late 30s or early 40s, who just looks incredibly old, like someone who's been living rough on the street for… years and years and years, in tattered clothes and pallid skin, unkempt, long hair missing in places, untrimmed, unwashed. Wild-eyed, moving frantically, almost animal-like, twitchy, with a basket on his lap, with a lid over the top of it, open just a crack, and he'll open it and look in, and then slam it back shut and look all around himself again, as if fearful that someone's watching.

DM: So, 3 doors: the child, the young adult, and the middle-aged… old man.
